name: FAO Schwarz
tierWhy: The company that ran the chain, FAO Inc., sold the name out of its second bankruptcy in January 2004, and the last original store, on Fifth Avenue, closed on July 15, 2015; the name now belongs to ThreeSixty Group, which opened a new, smaller flagship at 30 Rockefeller Plaza in November 2018 and was still running it in September 2026.[^8][^22][^26][^29][^30]

title: FAO Schwarz (1862–2015): two bankruptcies in one year
description: FAO Schwarz was a Fifth Avenue toy store. A catalog firm bought it with notes and stock in 2002 and went bankrupt twice in 2003. The flagship closed in 2015.

hero.dates: Founded in Baltimore in 1862. Parent bankrupt twice in 2003. Fifth Avenue flagship closed Jul 15, 2015.
hero.standfirst: Everyone wanted to own the most famous toy store in America. Nobody could make its chain of stores pay.
hero.deck: FAO Schwarz was the Fifth Avenue toy store from the film Big; a buyer paid for it with notes and stock in 2002, went bankrupt twice in 2003, and the flagship closed in 2015. It sold expensive toys from a showroom that tourists treated as an attraction, and from 1986 it tried to repeat that store in malls across the country. The Schwarz family sold out in 1963, and the business has been sold nine more times since. The buyer that mattered most was The Right Start, a small catalog retailer that bought 23 stores in January 2002 without paying cash, renamed itself FAO Inc. and filed for Chapter 11 twice in the following year. The flagship outlived it by eleven years. The account draws on the SEC filings of FAO Inc. and Toys “R” Us and on contemporary press. The years before 2001 rest on a reference history, and the page says so where that is the case.
hero.artCaption: Original illustration of a toy store with a red canopy and a toy-soldier doorman. Not an official asset; the lettering is left blank on purpose.

findings.title: The buyer was smaller than what it bought.
findings.text: The Right Start had total revenues of $53.6M in fiscal 2000. Within five months in 2001–02 it bought Zany Brainy and FAO Schwarz; in fiscal 2002 those two brands were 90.9% of its retail sales.[^1]

findings.title: No cash changed hands.
findings.text: The $35.95M purchase price for FAO Schwarz was $15.95M of notes and $20.0M of preferred stock. The deal brought in $407,000 of cash.[^1]

findings.title: The flagship model did not travel.
findings.text: FAO Inc. closed eight of the 23 stores it had bought within 16 months “because they did not perform as well as we expected.”[^1]

findings.title: Lenders and suppliers set the timetable.
findings.text: Suppliers stopped shipping in late 2002, and a notice of default on November 7, 2003 came 27 days before the second filing.[^6][^7][^12]

findings.title: The name was worth more than the stores.
findings.text: After 2004 only two stores survived, then one, then none. Toys “R” Us still booked a $45M gain selling the brand in 2016.[^8][^21][^24]
